transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-20
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood SE), Joan (Lodestar CTO), Ethan (Lodestar Eng Lead), Priya (Finance PM)

Summary:
Lodestar is evaluating Redwood for a customer-facing summarization and ticket-routing feature. Primary driver is cost predictability and staying within a tight monthly inference budget. They are weighing hosted (Redwood API) vs dedicated capacity vs private VPC for data residency. Key questions: per-token price sensitivity, impact of batching and KV cache on unit costs, how quantization/variant models affect latency and quality, and pilot scope/cost.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and traffic profile
- Per-token pricing mechanics / how we measure consumption
- Batching, KV/prefix cache and their realistic impact on per-call cost
- Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs (SLA, isolation, burst capacity)
- Pilot scope and success criteria
- Security/compliance pointers

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Joan (Lodestar): Hey, Joan here, CTO. Ethan's on for infra, Priya is on finance.
[00:12] Ethan (Lodestar): Hey all.
[00:13] Aisha: Great. Marcus and Lena from Redwood will talk through the cost surface. We're hoping to map the per-token economics to your traffic.
[00:21] Marcus (Redwood SE): Cool. Maybe a very high-level starting point: what's your current expected qps and average prompt length?
[00:27] Joan: We're looking at two flavors — an inline summarizer in our UI (high volume, short prompts, like 60 tokens output) and an async routing job that runs longer context (maybe 500-1k tokens). Peak for the summarizer could be ~120 rps, but average is more like 15–25.
[00:40] Priya (Lodestar - Finance PM): From finance perspective our monthly inference cap is around $18k to start. That's not flexible without exec signoff.
[00:47] Marcus: Understood. Two levers we usually point customers to: batching and prefix/KV caching. Batching raises throughput and lowers per-token compute cost, but increases latency slightly. KV cache reduces repeated context compute for sessions, which can dramatically cut per-session costs for multi-turn flows.
[01:05] Ethan: Quick question — caching only helps if we have repeated prefixes, right? Our use case is a lot of one-off inputs.
[01:11] Lena (Redwood): Yeah, caching benefits are workload dependent. For single-shot summarization it's minimal. For chat or multi-step pipelines where you re-use system prompts or user metadata, it can be significant.
[01:20] Joan: What about quantization? We want to understand quality tradeoffs if we go with int8 variants for cost savings.
[01:27] Marcus: Right — quantized variants (we call them q8/q4-ish) reduce GPU memory and increase throughput, lowering $/token. But you'll see a small quality delta, more pronounced on longer, creative outputs. For summarization models it's often acceptable but you'd want to run evals.
[01:42] Priya: Can you give ballpark per-token numbers?
[01:44] Marcus: For hosted, baseline unquantized model on XPU is roughly $0.000020 per input token and $0.000030 per output token — this is illustrative. Quantized paths can be 20–40% cheaper. With batching you can get effective cost down further depending on occupancy.
[02:00] Priya: So for a typical 60-token output and 20-token input, that is... math moment.
[02:05] Ethan: (mutters) 80 tokens total.
[02:06] Joan: That's ~0.0016? 
[02:08] Marcus: Around there. But two important caveats: first, we often bill per token consumed by the model variant served, and second, network overheads and small-model routing might adjust that.
[02:18] Aisha: Also we offer dedicated capacity which is a reserved pool — unit costs are lower there for committed throughput; and private deployments for stricter isolation (higher fixed fees). For Lodestar's budget, dedicated could make sense if you have sustained peak utilization.
[02:32] Joan: Our peaks are spiky — the UI summarizer is bursty. How does Redwood handle bursts with Dedicated?
[02:40] Marcus: Dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscaling rules. There's also a reserved baseline and a burst bucket you can configure; costs for bursts above reserved capacity are higher but still often cheaper than entirely hosted at peak.
[02:51] Ethan: How does batching affect user-perceived latency? We need under 300ms p95 for the inline summarizer ideally.
[02:58] Lena: Batching can add 20–120ms depending on queue window. For short outputs we recommend tiny window batching (5–10ms) with dynamic latency SLOs — you still get some throughput uplift. Also prefix cache removes tokens needing recomputation and can reduce p95 if you avoid re-running large contexts.
[03:17] Joan: Does Redwood expose the token-level telemetry so we can map cost back to product features?
[03:22] Aisha: Yes — Console shows per-route token breakdown, latency buckets, and cost by token type. You can split by model variant, route, or token role.
[03:30] Priya: On procurement — what's the pricing cadence? Monthly usage invoices? Any minimums?
[03:35] Aisha: Hosted is usage-based monthly with no minimum. Dedicated is committed monthly capacity with a minimum commit (we'll include specific tiers in the spreadsheet). Private has enterprise licensing plus infra costs.
[03:46] Ethan: For pilot scope, we'd like something that mimics our production peak for a week to see real unit costs. Is that feasible?
[03:52] Marcus: Absolutely. We can spin a pilot with a limited dedicated pool or hosted with reserved burst quota and run a 1k-request benchmark. Marcus: We'll use your prompt set and traffic shaping to replicate spikes.
[04:02] Joan: Security quick callouts — we need SSO, SAML, audit logs, and KMS integration for keys if private.
[04:09] Lena: We have SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and integrations with customer-managed KMS for Private. Hosted also supports encryption-at-rest and TLS in transit. We'll share SOC2 and the network diagram.
[04:19] Priya: How about data residency? Some of our EU customers require data not leave region.
[04:23] Aisha: We can pin model serving and storage to regions; Private (VPC) is preferred for strict residency. Hosted has region options but less isolation than VPC.
[04:32] Ethan: Any gotchas around KV cache and consistency if we use private on-prem?
[04:36] Marcus: On-prem gives you full control; KV cache behavior is deterministic. In hosted environments there are policies for cache TTLs and optional customer-specific cache partitions. We'll document those.
[04:46] Joan: One concern: do you throttle per-tenant or per-API-key? We need predictable SLOs for customers.
[04:51] Marcus: We can do token-level rate limits and per-customer reserved lanes in Dedicated. Hosted has quotas per API key but not the same isolation guarantees.
[04:58] Priya: From finance — can you model a scenario where dedicated reduces our $/token by 30% given our predicted volume?
[05:04] Marcus: We'll run a sensitivity model in the pricing sheet. We'll need your expected monthly tokens by route and peak shaping to be accurate.
[05:11] Ethan: We'll provide token histograms and a week of production traces.
[05:14] Joan: Timeline — we want to decide within 3 weeks and run a pilot in May. Any blockers?
[05:19] Aisha: That fits. Steps: Marcus will run the benchmark once you send prompts; Aisha will send pricing + sample contract; we'll schedule the SE deep dive.
[05:26] (brief crosstalk)
[05:30] Speaker 4: thanks everyone.
[05:32] Aisha: One more nuance — function calling and streaming can affect token patterns; if you stream outputs token-by-token you still incur cost per token but latency profile changes. Worth flagging if you plan to stream UI updates.
[05:44] Ethan: We do stream some short deltas; will that change cost materially?
[05:47] Marcus: It doesn't change total tokens, but streaming may impact latency perception and batching effectiveness. We'll test both modes.
[05:55] Joan: I appreciate the transparency. Can you also call out potential quality regression when switching to quantized variants so we can build evals?
[06:02] Marcus: Yes — we'll include a short eval harness and suggested thresholds (ROUGE/BLEU-like checks and human spot checks) to validate summarization quality.
[06:12] Aisha: All right, I'll recap next steps.
[06:15] Marcus: I'll own the benchmark and the sample pilot config.
[06:18] Aisha: I'll send pricing, contract, and security docs. Joan, ETA for prompt set?
[06:23] Joan: We can get that by end of day Thursday (2026-04-23).
[06:26] Priya: Finance will need a month-by-month forecast based on your sensitivity outputs.
[06:30] Aisha: We'll include a simple model in the spreadsheet.
[06:33] (meeting winds down)
